title: Preventing and managing heat stress in laying hens
subtitle: Keeping hens comfortable and productive through a UK summer heatwave.
excerpt: Chickens do not sweat; they shed heat by panting and by holding their wings away from their body. Once ambient temperature rises above 27 C, a laying flock will start to show the effects of heat stress: panting, reduced feed intake, thin-shelled eggs, and a sharp drop in laying rate. Heat stress above 35 C can be fatal.
sourceNotes: Gail Damerow, Storey's Guide to Raising Chickens (4th edn., 2017). Poultry World, Heat stress management UK (July 2022). AHDB Poultry, Managing Laying Hens in Hot Weather (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: Rapid open-beak breathing in poultry, the primary mechanism for releasing excess heat. Moderate panting on a hot day is normal; severe, continuous panting with wings held out is a sign of heat stress.
Mineral salts (sodium, potassium, chloride) added to drinking water to replace those lost through panting. Available as poultry-specific preparations.

content.text: UK summers are getting hotter and more unpredictable. A flock that coped fine for years may now face temperatures it has not encountered before. The management response is straightforward: shade, cold water, and ventilation. The time to set these up is before the heatwave, not during it.
with wings held away from the body.
Pale, limp comb and wattles. A normally red comb that looks dull or slightly blue is a warning sign.
Hens lying flat on shaded ground with feet extended.
Sharp drop in daily egg count; thin, rough shells; or loss of shell pigmentation.
Maximise shade in the run. Position a large tarpaulin or shade sail over the sunniest part of the run. Move any portable shelters to create shaded areas on the ground.

Provide additional water drinkers in the shade and refresh them with cold water two to three times per day. Hens drink significantly more in hot weather. An empty drinker on a 35 C day can cause rapid dehydration.

Open all coop ventilation fully at night and leave the pop-hole open if the run is predator-proof. Night is when the coop temperature should drop; a sealed coop in summer can be warmer inside than outside.
A hen that collapses from heat

A collapsed hen that is unresponsive but still breathing needs to be moved immediately to a cool, shaded place. Place her on a cool damp cloth. Offer cool (not ice-cold) water from a dropper to the side of the beak. Do not immerse her. If she does not recover within 15 to 20 minutes, call a vet.

attrs.cue: Egg production drops sharply during hot weather but no other symptoms visible
attrs.cause: Normal thermal response: hens divert energy away from egg production when body temperature is elevated
attrs.fix: This is a physiological response, not a disease. Production recovers once temperatures drop. Focus on shade and water management to reduce the impact.

attrs.cue: Hens crowding at the water drinker and others cannot access it
attrs.cause: Too few drinker points for the flock size
attrs.fix: Provide at minimum one drinker access point per 10 birds. In hot weather, one per 5 birds is better. Spread drinkers across the run in shaded locations.
